blocks.text: “Thanks, and thanks, and thanks again for your sweet letter. It was so nice to be able to tell you and to have your sympathy.

“My dear, things never seem to happen one at a time. They all come together, like heavy rain after the first few drops. How true these old sayings are! I shall be twenty in September. Yet until today, no one had ever really asked me to marry him. And today three men have asked me. Just imagine! THREE offers of marriage in one day! Isn’t it awful! I feel sorry, really and truly sorry, for two of the poor fellows. Oh, Mina, I am so happy that I don’t know what to do with myself. And three offers of marriage! But please, please don’t tell any of the girls. They would get all sorts of wild ideas. They would feel hurt and think men were treating them as unimportant unless at least six asked them on their very first day at home. Some girls admire themselves so much! You and I, Mina dear, are engaged. Soon we shall settle down and become serious old married women. We can look down on girls who think so much of themselves. Well, I must tell you about the three men. But you must keep it a secret, dear, from everyone except Jonathan, of course. You will tell him. I would certainly tell Arthur if I were in your place. A woman ought to tell her husband everything—don’t you think so, dear? And I must be fair. Men like women, certainly their wives, to be just as fair as they are. And I am afraid women are not always quite as fair as they should be. Well, my dear, the first man came just before lunch. I have told you about him: Dr. John Seward, the man from the hospital for people with mental illnesses. He has a strong jaw and a fine forehead. He seemed very calm, but he was nervous all the same. Clearly, he had practised all sorts of little things he should do, and he remembered them. But he almost sat down on his silk hat. Men don’t usually do that when they are calm. Then he tried to look relaxed by playing with a small surgical knife. The way he did it nearly made me scream. He spoke to me very directly, Mina. He told me how much he cared for me, although he had known me for so little time. He told me what his life would be like with me to help him and make him happy. He was going to tell me how unhappy he would be if I did not love him. But then he saw me cry. He said he was a brute and would not make me feel worse than I already did. Then he stopped and asked if I might come to love him in time. I shook my head, and his hands shook. Then, after hesitating a little, he asked if I already loved someone else. He asked very kindly. He said he did not want to force me to share my private feelings. He only wanted to know, because a man could hope if a woman did not already love someone. And then, Mina, I felt that I ought to tell him there was someone. That was all I told him. Then he stood up. He looked very strong and very serious as he took both my hands in his. He said he hoped I would be happy. If I ever needed a friend, I must think of him as one of my best. Oh, Mina dear, I can’t stop crying. You must forgive all the tear marks on this letter. It is very nice to have someone ask you to marry him, and all that. But it is not at all happy when you must watch a poor fellow leave looking completely heartbroken. You know he truly loves you. And whatever he may say at that moment, you know you are passing completely out of his life. My dear, I must stop here for now. I feel so unhappy, although I am so happy.

“Arthur has just gone, and I feel happier than when I stopped writing. So I can go on telling you about the day. Well, my dear, the second man came after lunch. He is such a nice fellow, an American from Texas. He looks so young and fresh. It seems almost impossible that he has visited so many places and had such adventures. I understand poor Desdemona’s feelings when a stream of stories about danger was poured into her ear, even by a black man. I suppose we women are such cowards that we think a man will save us from our fears. So we marry him. Now I know what I would do if I were a man and wanted a girl to love me. No, I don’t. There was Mr. Morris telling us his stories, while Arthur never told any, and yet—— My dear, I am getting ahead of my story. Mr. Quincey P. Morris found me alone. It seems a man always does find a girl alone. No, he doesn’t. Arthur tried twice to find a chance, and I helped him as much as I could. I am not ashamed to say it now. First, I must tell you that Mr. Morris doesn’t always use slang, those informal words people use when talking. He never uses it when speaking to strangers, or when strangers are there. He is really well educated and has wonderful manners. But he discovered that I enjoyed hearing him use American slang. Whenever I was there, and there was no one who might be shocked, he said such funny things. I am afraid, my dear, that he has to invent it all. It fits exactly with whatever else he wants to say. But slang does tend to do that. I don’t know whether I shall ever use slang myself. I don’t know whether Arthur likes it, as I have never heard him use any yet. Well, Mr. Morris sat beside me and looked as happy and cheerful as he could. But I could still see that he was very nervous. He took my hand in his and said so sweetly:—
